Joel 1.summary: The book opens by identifying the prophetic word as coming to Joel, son of Pethuel (Joel 1:1), but supplies no king or date. Joel summons elders and all inhabitants to remember and tell succeeding generations about an overwhelming calamity (Joel 1:2–3). Successive kinds or stages of locusts have consumed the crops (Joel 1:4); the devastation is described with imagery of an invading nation with lionlike teeth (Joel 1:6–7). Drinkers, farmers, vine dressers, and priests mourn because grain, wine, oil, and the produce of the land have failed (Joel 1:5–12). The shortage disrupts the grain and drink offerings at the house of the LORD (Joel 1:9), Joel 1:13. Joel calls priests to lament, proclaim a fast, and convene a solemn assembly to cry out to God (Joel 1:13–14). He names the approaching 'day of the LORD' as a time of destruction (Joel 1:15). The chapter ends with the prophet's cry to God as food, pasture, trees, and streams suffer, and even wild animals pant for water (Joel 1:16–20). Its main message is that a devastating communal crisis calls for serious lament and a collective turning toward God; the text does not give an independent historical date for the disaster.
Joel 1.whereWeAre: The chapter portrays catastrophic crop loss, devastation of fields, disrupted temple offerings, and distress among livestock and wild animals. Such losses are plausible in an ancient agrarian setting, but this particular event is not independently dated. A society depending on grain, grape harvests, olives, and flocks would feel devastation economically, socially, and religiously.

Joel 2.summary: Joel orders a trumpet alarm in Zion because the day of the LORD is near (Joel 2:1). He depicts an unstoppable, army-like force: darkness surrounds it, the land changes from gardenlike fertility to waste, and its advance resembles horses, chariots, and disciplined soldiers (Joel 2:2–11). Whether this imagery extends the locust plague, portrays human invaders, or deliberately combines both remains debated. Yet judgment is not the final appeal: God calls the people to return with all their heart, fasting, weeping, and mourning, and to 'rend your heart, and not your garments' (Joel 2:12–13). Joel summons all ages and social groups, including newly married couples, to assembly while priests plead for mercy (Joel 2:15–17). The text then describes the LORD's compassion, removal of the threatening force, renewal of the land, and restoration of grain, wine, and oil; the people will praise God and recognize the LORD in their midst (Joel 2:18–27). Finally, God promises to pour out the Spirit on sons and daughters, old and young, and male and female servants (Joel 2:28–29), accompanied by cosmic signs before the day of the LORD and a promise of deliverance for those who call on God's name (Joel 2:30–32). The chapter connects sincere repentance, promised restoration, and wider participation in God's Spirit; its images and fulfillment are read differently among religious traditions.
Joel 2.whereWeAre: The book imagines severe agricultural or military danger and addresses a gathered community; chapter 2 shifts from the alarm to repentance, restoration, and future prophecy. Trumpet warnings, solemn fasting, and petition at the temple fit the public religious life evoked by the oracle.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaker and actor within the prophetic message. Calls for heartfelt return, promises restoration, and announces the outpouring of the Spirit (2:12–14, 18–32)

keyFigures.name: People of Zion/Judah and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: Community receiving the alarm and the call to assembly. Urged to return and later promised renewal (2:1, 15–17, 23–27)

keyFigures.name: Priests and ministers of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Representatives in public worship. Directed to weep between the porch and altar and petition God for the people (2:17)

keyFigures.name: Children, elders, bridegroom, and bride
keyFigures.role: Groups explicitly summoned to communal assembly. Their inclusion underscores that the whole community is involved (2:16)

keyFigures.name: Sons, daughters, old men, young men, servants, and handmaids
keyFigures.role: Recipients named in the promised outpouring. Illustrate the promise extending across sex, age, and status (2:28–29)

keyFigures.name: Northern army/approaching host
keyFigures.role: Threatening force described in prophetic imagery. Its removal accompanies the announcement of compassion and restoration (2:20)

Joel 3.summary: The final chapter moves from Judah's promised restoration to the LORD's judgment of the nations (Joel 3:1–2). God summons nations to the 'valley of Jehoshaphat' because, according to the oracle, they scattered Israel, divided the land, cast lots for people, and traded children (Joel 3:2–3). Tyre, Sidon, and Philistine districts are accused of taking treasures and selling Judahites and Jerusalemites to Greeks; the prophetic speech announces a reversal of their actions (Joel 3:4–8). The nations are ironically commanded to prepare for war, even turning plowshares into swords, and to assemble for judgment (Joel 3:9–12). Harvest and winepress imagery express the fullness of wickedness and impending reckoning (Joel 3:13), while cosmic darkness accompanies the nearness of the day of the LORD (Joel 3:14–15). Yet the LORD is described as a refuge for his people and a stronghold for Israel, dwelling in Zion (Joel 3:16–17). The chapter closes with images of abundant wine, milk, water flowing from God's house, and enduring habitation in Judah and Jerusalem, set against desolation announced for Egypt and Edom (Joel 3:18–21). Its central contrast is judgment on oppressive nations and hope for Zion; details such as the valley's precise location and fulfillment timetable are not established by the text.
Joel 3.whereWeAre: The text accuses nations of displacement, territorial seizure, and trafficking, practices known broadly in ancient warfare. It does not provide enough detail to identify a particular independently verified incident behind every charge. The divine courtroom and assembly of nations turn Judah’s experience of loss into a wider picture of judgment and restoration.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Divine judge and refuge proclaimed by the prophet. Calls nations to account and promises to dwell in Zion (3:2, 12, 16–17, 21)

keyFigures.name: Israel, Judah, and Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The people and places at the center of the oracle. Portrayed as harmed by other nations and later restored (3:1–3, 16–21)

keyFigures.name: The nations
keyFigures.role: Collective parties summoned for judgment. Charged with scattering people and dividing land (3:2–3, 9–14)

keyFigures.name: Tyre, Sidon, and Philistine regions
keyFigures.role: Named neighboring peoples and places. Accused within the oracle of seizure of goods and human trafficking (3:4–8)

keyFigures.name: Greeks and Sabeans
keyFigures.role: Groups mentioned in trade and reversal imagery Greeks are named as buyers of exiles; Sabeans appear in the announced retaliatory sale (3:6, 8)

keyFigures.name: Egypt and Edom
keyFigures.role: Named nations in the closing oracle. Their desolation is contrasted with Judah’s enduring habitation (3:19–20)
